# Archive Pagination Specification

## Problem

The blog archive (`/blog/`) renders every post from `collections.posts` on a
single page. With several thousand posts this produces an unmanageably large
page for readers and an expensive HTML file.

## Intended behavior

The public archive is paginated at 20 posts per page, generated at build time
by Eleventy's pagination feature. The output remains fully static with zero
client-side JavaScript.

### URLs

- The first archive page keeps the existing address `/blog/`.
- Later pages use stable, sequential addresses: `/blog/page/2/`,
  `/blog/page/3/`, and so on. Page numbers are one-based and deterministic,
  derived only from the number of posts, so addresses do not change between
  builds unless post count changes across a page boundary.

### Ordering and coverage

- Posts appear newest-first on every archive page, matching the current
  archive ordering.
- Every post appears on exactly one archive page; no post is duplicated or
  omitted across the pagination set.

### Navigation

- Each archive page (except the first) links to the previous page.
- Each archive page (except the last) links to the next page.
- Previous/next links are plain `<a>` elements usable without JavaScript, and
  they use `rel="prev"`/`rel="next"` for assistive technology.
- The links are announced accessibly (e.g. "Previous page", "Next page") and
  remain keyboard reachable.

### Untouched behavior

The following keep their current behavior and URLs:

- Home page (`/`) and its list of latest posts.
- Tag pages and their per-tag post lists.
- Feed (`/feed/feed.xml`), which continues to draw from the full `posts`
  collection.
- Sitemap (`/sitemap.xml`), which continues to enumerate generated pages.
- Previous/next links between individual posts.

## Design

Convert `content/blog.njk` to use Eleventy pagination over the `posts`
collection with `size: 20`. The template's permalink becomes paginated so the
first page renders at `/blog/` and subsequent pages render under
`/blog/page/N/`. The page template reuses the existing `postslist.njk`
include, passing the current page's slice of posts in newest-first order.

# Archive pagination

Specification and requirements for paginating the public blog archive.
Status: specification complete, not implemented.

## Goal

Blogs with several thousand posts currently render the entire archive on a
single page at `/blog/`, which is unmanageably large. The archive should be
split into pages of 20 posts while keeping all existing behavior elsewhere
intact and the output static with zero client-side JavaScript.

## Design

Add Eleventy pagination to `content/blog.njk`:

- `pagination.data: collections.posts`, `size: 20`, and
  `pagination.reverse: true`, so pages are sliced from the newest end.
  The first page therefore shows the 20 newest posts, matching what a
  reader sees at the top of the current single-page archive.
- `collections.posts` is ordered oldest-first; the shared
  `_includes/postslist.njk` include reverses its input to display
  newest-first. The paged data must be supplied to that include in the
  ascending order it expects (or rendered directly newest-first) so the
  display is newest-first exactly once, not double-reversed.
- Permalink: the first page keeps `/blog/`; later pages use a stable
  pattern `/blog/page/N/` with `N` starting at 2 (e.g.
  `permalink: /blog/{{ pagination.pageNumber ? "page/" ~ (pagination.pageNumber + 1) ~ "/" : "index.html" }}`).
- Previous/next navigation between archive pages uses
  `pagination.href.previous` and `pagination.href.next`, rendered as real
  `<a>` elements with descriptive text (for example, "Newer posts" /
  "Older posts"). A link is omitted on the page where it does not exist:
  the first page has no "newer" link and the last page has no "older"
  link. No JavaScript is involved.
- The `eleventyNavigation` "Archive" metadata must apply only to the
  first page so no duplicate archive keys are produced.

Unchanged behavior:

- Home page (`content/index.njk`) keeps showing the 3 latest posts.
- Tag pages (`content/tag-pages.njk`) keep their existing pagination over
  `collections` (filtered to exclude `all` and `posts`).
- Feed (`feedPlugin`) keeps its current output and limit.
- Sitemap (`content/sitemap.xml.njk`) iterates `collections.all`, so it
  naturally gains entries for the new `/blog/page/N/` pages; all existing
  entries remain.
- Individual-post previous/next links
  (`getPreviousCollectionItem` / `getNextCollectionItem` on
  `collections.posts`) keep working across post boundaries, independent
  of archive pages.

Edge cases:

- Total pages is `ceil(post count / 20)`; the last page may contain fewer
  than 20 posts.
- With 20 or fewer posts only `/blog/` exists; no `/blog/page/2/` and no
  archive navigation are generated.
- Pagination slices are disjoint, so every post appears on exactly one
  archive page.

## Requirements

- [ ] R1: The archive is paginated into pages of 20 posts; the first page
      is served at the existing `/blog/` address.
- [ ] R2: Later archive pages exist at stable addresses
      `/blog/page/2/`, `/blog/page/3/`, … (1-indexed, 2 onward).
- [ ] R3: Posts are displayed newest-first within each archive page, and
      the first archive page shows the 20 newest posts.
- [ ] R4: Every post appears exactly once across all archive pages (no
      gaps, no duplicates).
- [ ] R5: Each archive page has accessible previous/next navigation:
      real anchor links with descriptive text, omitted where the target
      does not exist (none on the first "newer" side, none on the last
      "older" side).
- [ ] R6: The home page output is unchanged.
- [ ] R7: Tag page output is unchanged.
- [ ] R8: Feed output is unchanged.
- [ ] R9: Sitemap output keeps all existing URLs and gains the new
      archive page URLs.
- [ ] R10: Individual-post previous/next navigation is unchanged.
- [ ] R11: The build output remains static HTML with zero client-side
      JavaScript.

## State

- Specification: complete (this file).
- Implementation: not started.
- Verification: pending (verify R1–R11 after implementation by building
  the site and inspecting the generated archive pages, sitemap, feed, and
  a sample post).

# Archive pagination

Status: Proposed. This describes intended behavior and design; nothing is
implemented yet.

## Problem

With several thousand posts, the public archive renders every post on one
page at `/blog/`. The page becomes unmanageably large for readers to load
and scroll.

## Goal

Split the public blog archive into pages of 20 posts, preserving the site's
static, zero-JavaScript output and leaving every other surface unchanged.

## Intended behavior

### Pages and addresses

- The archive is split into `ceil(post count / 20)` pages.
- Page 1 keeps the existing address `/blog/`. It is the only address for the
  newest posts; `/blog/page/1/` is not generated.
- Page n (n ≥ 2) has the stable address `/blog/page/n/`. The address is
  derived only from the page number, so it stays the same when posts are
  added, edited, or removed.
- Pagination addresses must not collide with post addresses.

### Ordering and coverage

- Posts keep newest-first ordering. Page 1 holds the 20 newest posts, page 2
  the next 20, and so on; the last page holds the oldest remainder, which
  may be fewer than 20 posts.
- Within a page, posts render newest-first with the same list markup the
  archive uses today.
- Every post in `collections.posts` appears on exactly one archive page.

### Previous and next navigation

- Each archive page links to its adjacent pages with real `<a>` elements:
  - "Previous" on pages 2…N, linking to the previous page's address
    (`/blog/` for page 2, `/blog/page/n-1/` otherwise).
  - "Next" on pages 1…N-1, linking to `/blog/page/n+1/`.
- Page 1 has no previous link, the last page has no next link, and an
  archive of 20 posts or fewer remains a single page with no pagination
  controls.
- The links are keyboard operable, have discernible text such as
  "Previous page" and "Next page", carry `rel="prev"` / `rel="next"`, and
  sit inside a labelled navigation landmark.

### Unchanged behavior

- Home page: still lists the latest posts only; not paginated.
- Tag pages: one page per tag listing all matching posts; not paginated.
- Feed: `/feed/feed.xml` keeps its current content.
- Sitemap: keeps enumerating every generated page, so it lists `/blog/` and
  all later archive pages.
- Individual posts: previous/next links keep following full collection
  order.

## Design

- Use Eleventy's built-in pagination in `content/blog.njk`:
  - `data: "collections.posts"`, `size: 20`, with the data ordered
    newest-first before chunking (`reverse: true`, or a `before` callback
    that reverses the collection) so page 1 receives the newest posts.
  - `addAllPagesToCollections: true`, because pagination adds only the
    first page to collections by default; without it the sitemap, which
    reads `collections.all`, would miss pages 2 and later.
  - A `permalink` built from `pagination.pageNumber`: `/blog/` for the
    first page, `/blog/page/{pageNumber + 1}/` for the rest.
- Keep rendering posts through `_includes/postslist.njk` so the list markup
  stays identical. The include reverses its input for display, so pass each
  chunk in ascending order (for example `pagination.items | reverse`) to
  keep newest-first output.
- Render the previous/next links in `content/blog.njk` or a dedicated
  include used only by the archive.
- Keep the existing `eleventyNavigation` Archive entry attached to page 1
  only, so a rendered navigation would list the archive once.
- All pagination is resolved at build time. No client-side JavaScript is
  added; output remains static HTML.
- Later pages should be identifiable (for example a title or heading that
  mentions the page number); the exact wording is left open.

## Non-goals

- No pagination of the home page or tag pages.
- No change to feed, sitemap, or individual-post navigation behavior.
- No client-side JavaScript.
- This specification does not update user-facing documentation.

# Archive pagination specification

Status: Proposed

## Summary

Paginate the public blog archive into pages of 20 posts. Keep the first page
at `/blog/`, and publish later pages at stable, numbered URLs such as
`/blog/2/` and `/blog/3/`.

The archive remains a statically generated, newest-first list. Pagination
must not add a client-side runtime or change the URLs or ordering of
individual posts.

## Goals

- Make the archive page bounded and usable when the site contains thousands
  of posts.
- Keep `/blog/` as the address of the first archive page.
- Give every later archive page a deterministic, permanent address.
- Let keyboard and assistive-technology users move between adjacent archive
  pages.
- Preserve the complete archive: every post appears once, and only once,
  across the paginated pages.

## Archive model

1. Build the archive sequence from the same `collections.posts` source used by
   the current archive.
2. Normalize that sequence to the current display order, newest post first,
   before dividing it into pages.
3. Divide the sequence into contiguous groups of at most 20 posts.
4. Map the first group to `/blog/`. Map group `n` (where `n > 1`) to
   `/blog/n/`.
5. Render each group with the existing post-list presentation. A site with no
   posts still has the first archive route and renders an empty list; it does
   not produce later pages.

The page number is one-based and is part of the generated route, not a
client-side state value. Adding a newer post may change which existing page
contains older posts, but a given build always assigns pages deterministically
from the newest-first sequence.

## Pagination controls

Each archive page includes a semantic navigation region labelled for archive
pagination. It contains ordinary links to the immediately adjacent archive
pages:

- The first page has a next link when another page exists and no previous
  link.
- A middle page has both previous and next links.
- The last page has a previous link and no next link.

Links use descriptive, visible text (for example, “Previous page” and “Next
page”) and point directly to the corresponding trailing-slash route. The
The current page number is also conveyed in the navigation markup, with
`aria-current="page"` on its non-link indicator, for assistive technology;
there is no reliance on hover, color, or JavaScript. The controls are omitted
when the corresponding destination does not exist rather than rendered as
dead or misleading links.

## Compatibility boundaries

Pagination is limited to the public archive. The implementation must leave
the following behavior based on the complete posts collection unchanged:

- The home page continues to show its current number of latest posts.
- Tag pages continue to show their current collections and ordering.
- The feed continues to use its current collection and limit.
- The sitemap continues to be generated by its existing mechanism, with
  existing post URLs retained.
- Individual-post previous/next navigation continues to traverse the full
  post collection, not only posts on the current archive page.
- Generated output remains static and requires zero JavaScript.

This work does not define redirects, archive search, a page-number index, or
changes to current user documentation.

## Verification approach

Verification should build fixtures for zero, one, 20, 21, and a multi-page
post set, including posts with distinct dates and URLs. Inspect generated
files and assert:

- the route and post count for every archive page;
- newest-first order within and across page boundaries;
- the union of archive post URLs equals the source post URL set, with no
  duplicates;
- correct previous/next links at first, middle, and last boundaries;
- no script is required in generated archive HTML; and
- the home page, tag pages, feed, sitemap, and individual-post navigation
  retain their existing output and relationships.

# Paginated blog archive

## Status

Proposed. This document describes the intended behavior and design; it does
not describe an implemented change.

## Problem

The public archive at `/blog/` currently renders the complete `collections.posts`
collection in one page. That page becomes impractical to load and navigate when
the site contains several thousand posts.

## Scope

Change the public archive only. Partition its existing post collection into
pages of at most 20 posts while preserving the archive's current ordering and
the behavior of the other generated surfaces.

The change includes:

- static archive pages and their URLs;
- archive-page previous and next navigation;
- generation-time checks for page boundaries, ordering, completeness, and
  uniqueness.

The change does not include changing the home page, tag-page generation,
the feed, the sitemap template or contract, individual-post navigation, or
current user documentation.

## URL and pagination contract

- The first archive page remains `/blog/`.
- Later archive pages use stable, slash-terminated paths in the form
  `/blog/page/{number}/`, where `{number}` starts at `2` and increases by one.
  For example, the second and third pages are `/blog/page/2/` and
  `/blog/page/3/`.
- Archive pagination is path-based. It must not require query parameters,
  fragments, client-side routing, or client-side JavaScript.
- Page one is generated even when the collection is empty. The total number of
  pages for a non-empty collection is the ceiling of the post count divided by
  20.
- Each page contains no more than 20 post entries. The first page contains the
  newest posts, and each subsequent page continues through the collection in
  the same newest-first order.
- The final page may contain fewer than 20 entries.

The page-number URL is part of the public contract. Once emitted, a page's
address must remain derived from its archive position and must not depend on a
query string or browser state.

## Archive rendering and navigation

Each archive page continues to use the existing post-list presentation for its
entries. It also exposes a semantic archive-pagination navigation region:

- page one has a link to the next page when another page exists and no previous
  link;
- a middle page has links to both adjacent pages;
- the final page has a link to the previous page and no next link;
- links are ordinary, keyboard-focusable anchors with visible “Previous” and
  “Next” text (or equivalent text that identifies the destination);
- the navigation has an accessible name, such as
  `aria-label="Archive pagination"`, and the current page is conveyed in the
  rendered navigation or page context.

There must be no dead navigation links at either boundary. Navigation must
remain understandable and usable without CSS, hover behavior, or JavaScript.

## Collection invariants

The archive uses the same post population and effective date ordering as the
current archive. For a collection containing `N` posts:

1. Every post appears on exactly one archive page.
2. The concatenation of archive pages from page one through the final page is
   the existing newest-first archive order.
3. No page contains a duplicate post, and no post is omitted.
4. The first 20 posts in the existing archive order are on `/blog/`; the next
   20 are on `/blog/page/2/`; and so on.

These invariants must hold at page counts of one, two, and many pages,
including collections much larger than the target page size.

## Compatibility requirements

The following behavior remains unchanged:

- The home page keeps its current address, layout, and latest-post selection.
  In particular, it continues to show the current three latest posts rather
  than becoming an archive page.
- Tag pages continue to be generated from the existing tag collections, with

address `/blog/n/`. The address is deterministic from the page number and does
not require a query string, fragment, JavaScript state, or post slug.

page paths; inspect that page 2 and page 3 are `/blog/2/` and `/blog/3/`.

generate exactly `ceil(N / 20)` archive pages. Do not generate an empty final
page when `N` is divisible by 20.

Verification: build fixtures with 0, 1, 20, 21, and 40 posts and assert the
expected archive paths and page counts.

The concatenation of archive entries from page 1 through the final page is the

order, and compare the resulting post URL sequence with the expected
newest-first sequence.

Every post in `collections.posts` appears exactly once in the archive, and no
post outside that collection appears in the archive.

URLs equals the number of source posts.

sorting individual 20-post chunks must not cause an older chunk to appear
before a newer chunk.

archive ordering.

accessible label, text-bearing anchors, and no icon-only or script-only
controls.

from page 2 targets `/blog/`.

assistive technology. It does not rely on hover, focus side effects, disabled

accessible names and run the project's applicable accessibility checks.

HTML. Viewing, changing, or indexing an archive page does not require
client-side JavaScript.

per-page lists and links, and verify that disabling JavaScript does not change
archive rendering or navigation.

home page's post count or data source.

# Archive pagination specification

Status: Proposed

## Summary

Paginate the public blog archive into groups of 20 posts while keeping the
existing first-page URL, `/blog/`. Generate subsequent pages at deterministic
numeric URLs such as `/blog/2/` and `/blog/3/`. Every archive page is
pre-rendered by Eleventy and can be read and navigated without JavaScript.

This change applies only to the public archive. The home page, tag pages, feed,
sitemap, and individual-post navigation continue to use their existing
collections and behavior.

## Context and current behavior

`content/blog.njk` currently renders the complete `collections.posts`
collection in one page. The shared `postslist.njk` include reverses the
collection before rendering it, so the visible archive order is newest first.
That makes the archive output grow with the total number of posts.

The project is a static Eleventy site. The home page renders the three latest
posts, tag pages render their tag collection, the feed is limited to ten posts,
the sitemap enumerates `collections.all`, and post navigation is based on the
full `collections.posts` collection.

## Goals

- Limit each archive page to at most 20 posts.
- Preserve `/blog/` as the address of the first archive page.
- Give every later archive page a stable, bookmarkable, trailing-slash URL.
- Preserve the archive's global newest-first order.
- Include every post exactly once across the paginated archive.
- Provide visible, semantic previous and next navigation that works with
  keyboard navigation and assistive technology.
- Keep the generated result static and zero-JavaScript.
- Leave all non-archive surfaces and post URLs unchanged.

## Non-goals

- Do not paginate the home page, tag pages, feed, or sitemap.
- Do not change the number or ordering of posts on the home page.
- Do not change tag membership, feed configuration, sitemap generation, post
  permalinks, or individual-post previous/next relationships.
- Do not add client-side pagination, infinite scrolling, or a client-side
  post collection.
- Do not update current user documentation as part of this work.

## Public URL and page model

Use a one-based public page number:

| Archive page | Public URL |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | `/blog/` |
| 2 | `/blog/2/` |
| 3 | `/blog/3/` |
| `n`, where `n > 1` | `/blog/n/` |

The first page must not also be published as `/blog/1/`; that would create a
second public address for the same archive listing. Archive page URLs must not
depend on query strings, fragments, client state, or post slugs.

For `N` posts, generate exactly `max(1, ceil(N / 20))` archive pages. The
`/blog/` page remains available even when the collection is empty. Do not
generate an empty trailing page when `N` is an exact multiple of 20.

Page numbers are stable route identifiers. As with any ordinal archive, adding
newer posts may move a post to a different page; this does not change the
addressing rule or any individual post URL.

## Ordering and completeness

Treat the existing `collections.posts` ordering as authoritative and preserve
the same date/tie ordering currently used by the archive. Define the
newest-first archive sequence as `A`.

For archive page `n`, render the consecutive slice:

`A[(n - 1) * 20 ... n * 20]`

The first item on page 1 is therefore the current newest archive item, and the
last item on the final page is the current oldest archive item. No item may be
added, removed, or repeated while splitting the sequence into pages.

The current `postslist.njk` include reverses its input. The implementation must
reverse the complete source sequence before pagination, or explicitly preserve
the include's ordering contract when preparing each page. Reversing each
20-item chunk of an oldest-first pagination result is not sufficient, because
it would put older posts on earlier pages and violate the global newest-first
order.

## Archive navigation

Each generated archive page must contain a visible semantic navigation region
with an accessible label such as `Archive pagination`. Navigation links must
use text that communicates their destination, for example `Previous posts` and
`Next posts`; an icon alone is not sufficient.

- Page 1 has no previous link and, when another page exists, links next to
  `/blog/2/`.
- A middle page links previous to the immediately preceding page and next to
  the immediately following page.
- The final page has no next link.
- The previous link from page 2 targets `/blog/`, never `/blog/1/`.

The navigation must be ordinary static links in the generated HTML, usable by
keyboard and screen-reader users. It must not depend on disabled controls,
JavaScript event handlers, or dynamically fetched page content. Exposing the
current page and total page count is recommended where it improves orientation,
provided it does not replace the previous and next links.

## Static generation design

Use Eleventy build-time pagination over the full posts collection with a page
size of 20 and a deterministic permalink function implementing the URL model
above. Pagination must happen after establishing the newest-first source
sequence, not after taking arbitrary oldest-first chunks.

Each page must contain its own complete archive list and navigation links in
the generated HTML. A request for `/blog/2/` must not require the browser to
load `/blog/` first, execute a script, or fetch an API. No pagination runtime,
hydration code, or JavaScript-only control is part of this design.

The existing sitemap contract remains in place: `/sitemap.xml` is generated
from `collections.all` and is not replaced with a paginated or truncated
collection. The generated archive pages are ordinary public Eleventy pages and
therefore remain subject to that existing sitemap enumeration.

## Compatibility constraints

The implementation must preserve these existing behaviors:

- The home page continues to show the same three latest posts in the same
  order.
- Each tag page continues to show all posts in that tag with its current URL
  and ordering.
- The feed remains at `/feed/feed.xml`, continues to use the `posts`
  collection and its current limit of ten posts, and keeps its current
  ordering.
- The sitemap remains at `/sitemap.xml` and continues to enumerate public
  generated pages through `collections.all`.
- Individual-post previous and next navigation continues to be calculated
  from the full, unpaginated `collections.posts` collection. Archive page
  boundaries must not become post-navigation boundaries.
- Individual post URLs and the existing archive page title/list presentation
  remain unchanged except for the addition of page-specific navigation.

landmark with the accessible label `Archive pagination`.

- a previous link shall exist only when `p > 1` and shall target the route for
  page `p - 1` (the route for page 1 is `/blog/`);
- a next link shall exist only when another page follows and shall target
  `/blog/(p + 1)/`;
- previous links shall identify the newer archive page and use `rel="prev"`;
- next links shall identify the older archive page and use `rel="next"`;

  current page.

Previous and next controls shall have meaningful visible text containing
“Previous” and “Next”; their meaning shall not depend on an icon, CSS, or
JavaScript. Each archive page shall expose a text position indicator such as
“Page `p` of `total`”, and the current page shall not be represented as a
pagination link.

Verification: inspect the rendered text and accessibility tree, and confirm
that the controls are reachable and understandable by keyboard and
screen-reader navigation.

The complete archive and its navigation shall be usable with JavaScript
disabled. All archive pages and links shall be present in the build output;
the archive shall not depend on client-side pagination, DOM mutation, fetch,
hydration, or a script-generated fallback.

Verification: inspect generated archive HTML for pagination scripts and
exercise the route links with JavaScript disabled.

current order, with its current post URLs and without archive pages being
included as posts.

after the implementation.

one-page-per-tag pagination behavior shall remain unchanged. Archive page

pagination shall not add archive pages to the feed or reduce the feed to the

the implementation to satisfy AP-001 through AP-014 and the boundary,
accessibility, static-output, and regression checks described above. No current

# Public archive pagination specification

Status: Proposed

## Purpose

The public archive currently renders the complete `collections.posts`
collection at `/blog/`. As the number of posts grows, that produces an
unmanageably large document. This change paginates that archive at build time
while keeping the site a static, zero-JavaScript publication.

The archive is the only target of this change. The existing home page, tag
pages, feed, sitemap, and individual-post navigation remain separate consumers
of the existing collections and retain their current behavior.

The associated acceptance requirements are in
[archive-pagination-requirements.md](archive-pagination-requirements.md).

## Page model and URLs

The generator creates one archive document for every group of 20 published
posts:

- The first page keeps the existing `/blog/` URL. `/blog/1/` is not generated.
- Page 2 is `/blog/2/`, page 3 is `/blog/3/`, and so on.
- Later-page URLs use trailing slashes and contain no query-string state.
- With `N` posts, the number of archive pages is
  `max(1, ceil(N / 20))`. An empty archive still has `/blog/`, with an empty
  list and no previous or next link.
- The page-number-to-URL mapping is deterministic and does not depend on
  client-side state.

These routes are the public, stable addresses for the archive pages. The
existing `/blog/` route must not move or become a redirect to a numbered
route.

## Content and ordering

Pagination uses the same published-post collection as the current archive.
It must not create a second definition of what qualifies as a post or change
the collection's ordering for other consumers.

The effective archive sequence is newest first, matching the current archive's
visible order. Page 1 contains the first 20 posts in that sequence; each later
page contains the next 20. The sequence formed by reading page 1 through the
last page, and each page from top to bottom, is therefore exactly the sequence
that the current unpaginated archive displays.

The existing `postslist.njk` presentation reverses its input. The eventual
implementation must coordinate pagination with that presentation detail so
that it does not reverse each page or the page order accidentally. In
particular, slicing an older-to-newer collection and then independently
reversing each slice must not make page 1 oldest-first or reorder posts across
page boundaries.

Every published post has exactly one archive occurrence across all generated
archive pages. A post must not be duplicated at a page boundary, and no post
may be omitted because it falls outside a page-local slice.

## Archive navigation

Each generated archive page exposes a semantic pagination landmark:

```html
<nav aria-label="Archive pagination">…</nav>
```

The controls use ordinary server-rendered links and have meaningful visible
names:

- “Previous” points to the lower-numbered archive page, which contains newer
  posts. Page 1 has no previous link.
- “Next” points to the higher-numbered archive page, which contains older
  posts. The final page has no next link.
- A link is omitted at a boundary rather than rendered as a disabled or empty
  anchor.
- The links use `rel="prev"` and `rel="next"` consistently with those
  destinations. Their names remain understandable to a keyboard user or
  screen-reader user without relying on an icon.
- The navigation includes a text page position such as “Page 2 of 8” so a
  reader can identify the current position in the archive. The current page
  itself is not presented as a link.

The navigation must work in document order with normal keyboard controls and
must not require focus management, client-side routing, or a script.

## Compatibility boundaries

The archive pagination is scoped to `content/blog.njk` and its archive
presentation. It must preserve these existing behaviors:

| Area | Behavior to preserve |
| --- | --- |
| Home page | `content/index.njk` continues to show the current three latest posts in its existing order and URLs. |
| Tag pages | `content/tag-pages.njk` continues to generate the existing tag pages and lists from each tag collection, including its current pagination behavior. |
| Feed | The feed remains at `/feed/feed.xml`, uses the `posts` collection, and retains its current 10-post limit and ordering. Archive page generation must not make the feed consume archive pages or a 20-item slice. |
| Sitemap | `/sitemap.xml` remains a static all-page listing generated by the existing sitemap mechanism. It must not be paginated or use archive-page slices. The new public archive URLs may appear as additional entries under the existing `collections.all` rule; existing sitemap URLs and serialization behavior must remain intact. |
| Individual posts | Previous/next post navigation continues to use the full `collections.posts` sequence, with its current direction, labels, and targets. A post at an archive-page boundary must still link to its adjacent post rather than to an archive page. |

No post permalink, tag permalink, feed permalink, sitemap permalink, or
individual-post navigation rule is changed by this specification.

## Static output constraint

All archive pages, post lists, page-position text, and previous/next links are
generated during the Eleventy build. The emitted archive HTML contains no
client-side pagination logic, fetch step, hydration requirement, or
JavaScript-dependent fallback. A reader with JavaScript disabled can browse
from `/blog/` through the final archive page using the same links.

## Verification approach

Verification should build the site with post fixtures at the important
boundaries: 0, 1, 19, 20, 21, 40, and 41 posts, plus a substantially larger
collection. For each build, verify:

1. The route count and exact route names match the page model.
2. Every archive page contains no more than 20 post entries.
3. Concatenated post URLs are newest-first and equal the source post URLs with
   no missing or repeated URL.
4. Previous/next links and page-position text are correct at the first,
   middle, and final pages.
5. The archive output has no script or client-side pagination dependency.
6. Existing home-page, tag-page, feed, sitemap, and individual-post URL and
   content invariants still hold.

The implementation is out of scope for this document. Current user
documentation is also out of scope; this specification and its requirements
are development documentation only.

# Notes Pagination

## Specification

`GET /notes/` returns every note as a plain JSON array. For large note
collections this makes responses slow and unnecessarily large. This
specification adds optional pagination to `GET /notes/` without changing the
response body shape or any other endpoint.

### Query parameters

| Parameter | Type | Constraint | Default |
|-----------|------|------------|---------|
| `limit` | int | 1–100 inclusive | absent |
| `offset` | int | 0 or greater | absent |

Both parameters are optional. When neither is provided, the endpoint must
return the current full-list response exactly as it does today.

### Behavior

- When pagination is requested, results are ordered by ascending note `id`,
  so paging with a given `limit` and `offset` is stable across requests.
- The response body remains the existing JSON array of note objects; no
  envelope or metadata object is introduced.
- For paginated responses, the total number of notes in the collection is
  exposed through the `X-Total-Count` response header.
- Invalid parameter values (for example `limit=0`, `limit=101`, or
  `offset=-1`) are rejected by FastAPI's normal request-validation handling
  with a 422 response.
- All other note endpoints (`GET /notes/{id}/`, `POST /notes/`,
  `PUT /notes/{id}/`, `DELETE /notes/{id}/`) remain unchanged.

### Design

# Notes pagination specification

`GET /notes/` returns every note as a plain JSON array. Large note collections
make these responses slow and unnecessarily large. This specification defines
optional pagination for that endpoint without changing its existing response
shape or any other note endpoint.

## Overview

`GET /notes/` accepts two optional query parameters:

| Parameter | Type    | Constraints          | Default     |
|-----------|---------|----------------------|-------------|
| `limit`   | integer | 1–100 inclusive      | unset       |
| `offset`  | integer | zero or greater      | unset       |

When neither parameter is supplied, the endpoint keeps its current behavior and
returns the full list of notes. When pagination is requested, the endpoint
returns a window of the notes in stable ascending note-ID order and reports the
total note count in an `X-Total-Count` response header.

## Intended behavior

### Backward compatibility

A request without `limit` and without `offset` must behave exactly as it does
today: a `200` response whose body is the existing JSON array of all note
objects, in the order the endpoint currently produces, with no additional
required response headers. Requests that supply only one of the two parameters
are also treated as paginated requests, with the other parameter at its
conceptual default (`limit` unset means no row cap within the page rules;
`offset` unset means offset 0).

### Paginated requests

When `limit` or `offset` is supplied:

- Results are ordered by ascending note `id`. This order is stable: repeated
  requests with the same parameters return the same notes in the same order.
- `limit` bounds the maximum number of notes returned. Valid values are
  integers from 1 through 100 inclusive.
- `offset` is the zero-based number of notes to skip before the first returned
  note. Valid values are integers greater than or equal to 0.
- The response body remains the existing array of note objects; the array
  contains at most `limit` notes starting at the `offset` position in ascending
  ID order. An `offset` at or beyond the end of the collection yields an empty
  array with status `200`.
- The response includes an `X-Total-Count` header whose value is the total
  number of notes in the collection, independent of `limit` and `offset`.

### Validation

Invalid pagination values — for example, `limit` of 0, 101, or a non-integer, or
a negative `offset` — must produce FastAPI's normal `422 Unprocessable Entity`
validation response. No custom error format is introduced.

### Unchanged endpoints

`GET /notes/{id}/`, `POST /notes/`, `PUT /notes/{id}/`, and
`DELETE /notes/{id}/` are unchanged by this specification.

## Design notes

- `limit` and `offset` are declared as optional integer query parameters on the
  `read_all_notes` route using FastAPI's `Query` validation (`ge=1, le=100` for
  `limit`; `ge=0` for `offset`), so constraint violations surface through the
  framework's standard validation response.

  array-of-note-objects body shape.
- `X-Total-Count` is added to paginated responses via the route's `Response`
  parameter; unpaginated responses need not include it.
- The data layer gains a way to fetch a bounded, ID-ordered window of notes plus
  the total note count, so paginated queries do not load the full collection.

## Requirements

- R1: `GET /notes/` with neither `limit` nor `offset` returns the current
  full-list response: status `200` with the existing JSON array of note objects
  and no behavioral change.
- R2: When `limit` or `offset` is supplied, results are returned in stable
  ascending note-ID order.
- R3: `limit` must be an integer between 1 and 100 inclusive; values outside
  that range are rejected with FastAPI's normal `422` validation response.
- R4: `offset` must be an integer greater than or equal to 0; negative or
  non-integer values are rejected with FastAPI's normal `422` validation
  response.
- R5: The response body for paginated requests remains the existing array of
  note objects, containing at most `limit` notes starting `offset` positions
  into the ascending-ID ordering.
- R6: Paginated responses include an `X-Total-Count` header carrying the total
  number of notes in the collection, independent of `limit` and `offset`.
- R7: The other note endpoints (`GET /notes/{id}/`, `POST /notes/`,

### Current behavior

- `GET /notes/` accepts no query parameters and returns `200` with a JSON
  array containing every note. Each note has the fields `id`, `title`, and
  `description` (the `NoteDB` shape).
- The response carries no `X-Total-Count` header and the database query has no
  explicit ordering, so row order is not guaranteed.

### Proposed behavior

`GET /notes/` gains two optional query parameters:

| Parameter | Type             | Constraint        | Default when omitted |
|-----------|------------------|-------------------|----------------------|
| `limit`   | optional integer | 1 <= `limit` <= 100 | 100                |
| `offset`  | optional integer | `offset` >= 0     | 0                    |

When both parameters are omitted, the response is exactly the current
full-list response: status `200`, a JSON array containing every note, and no
`X-Total-Count` header.

When either parameter is supplied, the response is paginated:

- Notes are ordered by ascending `id`, so the ordering is stable across
  requests and consecutive pages partition the note set without gaps or
  overlap.
- At most `limit` notes are returned, skipping the first `offset` notes of
  that ordering. An `offset` at or beyond the total count yields an empty
  array.
- The response body remains the existing JSON array of note objects with the
  same `NoteDB` fields. No envelope or metadata object is introduced.
- The response includes an `X-Total-Count` header holding the total number of
  notes, not the number of notes in the current page.

`offset`, or a non-integer value — are rejected by FastAPI's normal request
validation, producing its standard `422` validation response. No custom error
body is added.

All other endpoints (`GET /notes/{id}/`, `POST /notes/`,
`PUT /notes/{id}/`, `DELETE /notes/{id}/`) remain unchanged in behavior,
status codes, and response headers.

- Validate with `fastapi.Query` constraints (`ge`/`le`) on optional integer
  parameters, so invalid input produces FastAPI's standard `422` response
  without custom checks.
- Treat "both parameters are `None`" as the trigger for the unchanged

  obtain the total for `X-Total-Count`.

  `response_model=List[NoteDB]` and the array body shape are untouched.

  behavior for requests without pagination.

# Notes list pagination specification

Status: Proposed

This document describes a future change to `GET /notes/`. It is a development
specification only; it does not implement the change or update current
user-facing documentation.

## Purpose and scope

Large note collections should be retrievable in bounded pages when a caller
requests pagination, while existing callers that send no pagination
parameters continue to receive the current full list. The change is limited
to `GET /notes/`. The create, read-one, update, and delete note endpoints,
their schemas, and their existing status and error behavior are out of scope.

## Request contract

`GET /notes/` accepts these optional query parameters:

| Parameter | Type | Valid values | Omitted behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `limit` | Integer | At least `1` and at most `100`, inclusive | No row limit is applied |
| `offset` | Integer | `0` or greater | Starts at the first row when `limit` is supplied |

Pagination mode is active whenever either parameter is present, including
`offset=0`. The parameter combinations have these meanings:

| Query parameters | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Neither parameter | Return the existing full list, preserving the current unpaginated response contract |
| `limit` only | Return at most `limit` notes starting at offset `0` |
| `offset` only | Return notes starting at `offset` through the end of the collection |
| Both parameters | Return at most `limit` notes starting at `offset` |

For every paginated request, notes must be selected in stable ascending
numeric `id` order before applying `offset` and `limit`. An offset beyond the
end of the collection therefore produces an empty array, while remaining a
valid request.

## Response contract

The response body remains a JSON array of the existing note objects. It must
not be replaced with an envelope containing `items`, `total`, or pagination
links. Each returned object retains the existing `id`, `title`, and
`description` fields.

Every successful paginated response includes the `X-Total-Count` header. Its
value is the decimal total number of notes in the collection before applying
the requested offset or limit, including when the returned page is empty.
The header is not part of the unpaginated response contract.

Requests with neither parameter continue to return the complete collection
through the existing full-list behavior. They do not acquire pagination
ordering or the `X-Total-Count` header as part of this change.

## Validation and errors

FastAPI's normal query-parameter validation must enforce the bounds:

- `limit=0`, a negative limit, or a limit greater than `100` is invalid.
- A negative offset is invalid.
- Values that cannot be parsed as integers are invalid.

Invalid pagination values must produce FastAPI's normal validation response
(HTTP `422` with its standard validation error shape). No custom pagination
error format is required.

## Data-access design

For a paginated request, the data layer should perform the ordering and
offset/limit selection in the database query rather than loading the entire
collection and slicing it in application memory. The total should come from a
count query over the complete notes collection and must not be reduced to the
page length. The existing no-parameter path should retain its current
full-list behavior.

## Compatibility and non-goals

- `GET /notes/{id}/`, `POST /notes/`, `PUT /notes/{id}/`, and
  `DELETE /notes/{id}/` remain unchanged.
- The note object schema, list response shape, and existing endpoint status
  and error behavior remain unchanged.
- Cursor pagination, filtering, response envelopes, and a default page size
  are not introduced by this specification.
- Current user-facing documentation is not updated as part of this
  specification-only task.

See the [notes list pagination requirements](notes-pagination-requirements.md)
for the acceptance requirements and verification scenarios.

# Book filter specification

A user-facing filter on the Books page lets readers switch between All,
Read, and Unread books. The All view is the initial view and matches the
current behavior of listing every book.

## Behavior

### Filter selection

The Books page presents three filter options: All, Read, and Unread.

- All is selected initially, so the page loads with the existing all-books
  collection.
- Selecting Read requests only books whose read status is true.
- Selecting Unread requests only books whose read status is false.
- Selecting All requests the unfiltered collection, identical to the
  current response.

### Server query parameter

The server exposes the filter through an optional `read` query parameter
on `GET /books`.

- `GET /books` (no `read` parameter) returns the current all-books
  response, unchanged.
- `GET /books?read=true` returns only books with `read` equal to true.
- `GET /books?read=false` returns only books with `read` equal to false.

The JSON response shape is preserved: the same `status` and `books` keys
are returned for filtered and unfiltered requests. Filtered responses
contain a subset of the same book objects; no new fields, nesting, or
envelope changes are introduced.

### Filter persistence across list refreshes

The selected filter remains active when the list refreshes after add,
update, and delete operations.

- Each mutation request (add, update, delete) is followed by a refresh of
  the list using the currently selected filter, so the server request
  carries the same `read` parameter as the last user selection.
- Adding a Read book while the Read filter is active keeps the new book
  visible; adding an Unread book while the Read filter is active leaves
  the list unchanged for that refresh.
- Updating a book so that it no longer matches the active filter removes
  it from the displayed list on refresh.
- Deleting a book refreshes the remaining books under the active filter.

### Empty results

When no books match the active filter, the page shows a clear empty
result state.

- The empty state identifies that no books match the selected filter
  (for example, "No Unread books" when the Unread filter is active and
  the filtered collection is empty).
- The empty state appears only when the filtered collection is empty; it
  does not replace the table when books match.

## Design

### Vue client

- `Books.vue` holds the selected filter in component state, initialized
  to All.
- The template renders the three filter options bound to that state.
- `getBooks()` sends the `read` query parameter only when the selected
  filter is Read (`read=true`) or Unread (`read=false`); for All it
  issues the same request as today, with no `read` parameter.
- The mutation helpers (`addBook`, `updateBook`, `removeBook`) keep
  calling `getBooks()` after their server request, so the refresh
  automatically reuses the current filter selection without duplicated
  filter logic.

### Flask server

- The `GET` branch of the `/books` route reads the optional `read` query
  parameter from `request.args`.
- When `read` is absent, the route returns the full `BOOKS` list exactly
  as before.
- When `read` is `true` or `false`, the route returns the books whose
  `read` field matches that value.
- The response continues to be `jsonify({"status": "success", "books":
  ...})`; the filtered list is placed in the existing `books` key.

### Compatibility

- `POST /books`, `PUT /books/<book_id>`, and `DELETE /books/<book_id>`
  keep their current request and response behavior; the filter touches
  only the `GET /books` branch.
- Clients that call `GET /books` without the `read` parameter observe no
  change in response shape or content.
- Requests with a `read` value other than `true`/`false` are out of scope
  for the initial implementation; omitting the parameter remains the only
  way to request all books.

## Requirements

1. The Books page offers All, Read, and Unread filter options, with All
   selected on initial load.
2. Selecting Read fetches `GET /books?read=true` and displays only books
   with `read: true`.
3. Selecting Unread fetches `GET /books?read=false` and displays only
   books with `read: false`.
4. Selecting All fetches `GET /books` without the `read` parameter and
   displays all books, matching the current behavior.
5. `GET /books` without `read` returns the unchanged all-books response.
6. `GET /books?read=true` and `GET /books?read=false` return only the
   matching books, using the existing `status`/`books` JSON shape.
7. The selected filter persists across the list refresh triggered by
   add, update, and delete operations.
8. When no books match the active filter, the page shows a clear empty
   result state naming the selected filter.
9. Existing CRUD behavior (POST, PUT, DELETE, and unfiltered GET) remains
   compatible for current clients.

## Purpose

Add a user-facing filter to the Vue Books page so readers can switch between
all books, read books, and unread books. Filtering is performed by the Flask
server, while the Vue client owns the selected filter and requests the
corresponding collection.

## Scope

This change covers:

- a three-option filter on the Books page: All, Read, and Unread;
- an optional `read` query parameter on `GET /books`;
- server-side filtering of the existing book collection;
- retaining the selected filter during add, update, and delete refreshes; and
- a clear empty result when the selected collection contains no books.

Book creation, update, and deletion remain the existing operations. This
change does not add a second response format, change the book fields, or
change current user documentation.

## Behavior

### Filter selection

The Books page initially selects **All**. Selecting a filter makes it the
active filter and reloads the list from the server:

| User-facing option | Request |
| --- | --- |
| All | `GET /books` |
| Read | `GET /books?read=true` |
| Unread | `GET /books?read=false` |

The client should use the existing `read` boolean field on each book. A book
is Read when `read` is `true` and Unread when `read` is `false`.

The active selection is page state, not a one-time request option. After a
successful add, update, or delete, the client reloads using the same request
mapping. For example, a user on Unread remains on Unread after deleting a
book.

### API contract

`GET /books` continues to return the current JSON envelope:

```json
{
  "status": "success",
  "books": [
    {
      "id": "1",
      "title": "On the Road",
      "author": "Jack Kerouac",
      "read": true
    }
  ]
}
```

When `read` is omitted, the endpoint returns all books, preserving the
current response and behavior. When `read=true`, it returns only books whose
`read` field is `true`. When `read=false`, it returns only books whose `read`
field is `false`. Filtering changes only the contents of `books`; the
`status` field and book object shape remain unchanged.

The parameter is optional so existing clients and the All view remain
compatible. The implementation should treat `true` and `false` as the
supported boolean query values and should define a consistent client-visible
error behavior for unsupported values rather than silently selecting the
wrong collection.

POST `/books` and PUT/DELETE `/books/<book_id>` retain their existing routes,
payload expectations, and response compatibility. The filter applies to
collection reads only.

### Empty results

The page must render an explicit empty-result state when the server returns an
empty `books` array for the active filter. The state should identify that no
books match the selected filter and should not be confused with a loading
state or an API failure. The state applies to All as well as Read and Unread.

## Client design

The Vue component should keep a single active-filter value and derive the
request query from it. The initial value must map to an omitted `read`
parameter. Filter selection and all CRUD refreshes must call the same
collection-loading path so the selected value cannot be lost.

The filter control should expose the three options with an unambiguous active
state and should remain usable after an empty result. The existing book table
continues to display the returned books and their title, author, and read
status.

## Verification approach

Verification should cover the API mapping and the page lifecycle:

1. Check that an omitted parameter returns the unfiltered collection and the
   existing JSON shape.
2. Check that `read=true` and `read=false` return only their matching books,
   including an empty `books` array when there are no matches.
3. Check that the initial Vue request is the All request.
4. Check that switching options issues the matching request and updates the
   active state and rows.
5. For each add, update, and delete operation, check that the follow-up
   request preserves the active filter.
6. Check that the empty-result state is shown for an empty filtered response.
7. Check that existing CRUD routes and unfiltered clients remain compatible.

# Books filter specification

## Purpose

Allow readers to choose which books are shown on the Books page without
changing the existing CRUD workflow. The page will support three views:
**All**, **Read**, and **Unread**.

## Scope

This change covers:

- the filter control and empty state in the Vue Books component;
- the optional `read` query parameter on `GET /books`;
- preserving the selected filter when the client reloads books after a
  successful add, update, or delete.

Book creation, update, deletion, and the existing response format remain
unchanged.

## User experience

The Books page presents a clearly labelled filter control with these choices:

| Choice | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| All | Show every book |
| Read | Show books whose `read` value is `true` |
| Unread | Show books whose `read` value is `false` |

**All** is selected when the page is first opened. Changing the choice
reloads the collection from the server and replaces the table contents with
the selected collection. The control remains on the selected choice while
the request and subsequent refresh complete.

When the selected collection contains no books, the page displays a clear
empty-result message, such as “No books match this filter.” The empty state
must distinguish an empty result from a loading failure and must not render a
misleading blank table as the only indication.

## Client behavior

The Books component owns the current filter as state. Its initial state is
`All`.

Every collection request uses the current filter:

- `All`: `GET /books` with no `read` parameter;
- `Read`: `GET /books?read=true`;
- `Unread`: `GET /books?read=false`.

The client should centralize this mapping in the collection-loading path so
initial loading, filter changes, and CRUD-triggered reloads use the same
behavior.

After a successful add, update, or delete, the client reloads books using the
currently selected filter rather than resetting to `All`. Consequently, a
new or updated book appears only when it belongs to the active collection,
and a deleted book is removed from the displayed collection. Existing CRUD
actions and their payloads remain compatible.

## Server behavior

`GET /books` accepts an optional `read` query parameter:

| Request | Collection returned |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /books` | All books |
| `GET /books?read=true` | Books with `read == true` |
| `GET /books?read=false` | Books with `read == false` |

Filtering is performed on the server before the response is serialized. The
unfiltered request remains the compatibility path: omitting `read` returns
the current all-books collection.

All three requests preserve the existing JSON envelope and book shape:

```json
{
  "status": "success",
  "books": [
    {
      "id": "1",
      "title": "On the Road",
      "author": "Jack Kerouac",
      "read": true
    }
  ]
}
```

The `status` field and `books` array remain present even when the filtered
array is empty. POST `/books` and PUT/DELETE `/books/<book_id>` retain their
existing routes and behavior.

## Interaction and failure considerations

The filter control should not mutate a book or alter CRUD payloads. A
collection reload caused by changing the filter or completing a CRUD action
must use the latest selected filter. If a request fails, the existing client
error-handling convention should apply; this feature does not redefine CRUD
or API error responses.

## Verification outline

Verification should cover:

1. Initial page load selects All and requests the unfiltered endpoint.
2. Read and Unread each issue the matching query and display only matching
   books.
3. An omitted query returns the same envelope and all-books behavior as
   before.
4. A filtered empty collection renders an explicit empty-result message.
5. Add, update, and delete each reload using the active filter.
6. Existing CRUD routes, payloads, and response handling remain compatible.

# Books page filter specification

## Status

Proposed. This document describes the intended behavior and design; it does
not describe an implemented feature.

## Objective

Allow readers to switch the Books page between all books, books marked as
read, and books marked as unread. Filtering is performed by the Flask API so
the Vue client always renders the collection returned by the server.

## User experience

The Books page provides one mutually exclusive filter control with these
options:

| Label | Client state | Request |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All | `all` | `GET /books` |
| Read | `read` | `GET /books?read=true` |
| Unread | `unread` | `GET /books?read=false` |

The following behavior applies:

- `All` is selected when the page is first opened.
- Selecting a filter immediately loads the corresponding collection and
  marks that filter as active.
- The active filter remains selected while the collection is loading and
  after the response is rendered.
- A successful add, update, or delete operation reloads the collection using
  the currently active filter. The operation must not reset the page to
  `All`.
- If the selected collection is empty, the page displays a clear empty-result
  message, such as `No books match this filter.` The page must not leave
  stale rows from the previous collection visible.
- When the selected collection contains books, the existing title, author,
  and read-status columns remain available.

The filter control is part of the Books page and does not change the existing
book add, edit, or delete interactions.

## Flask API design

`GET /books` accepts an optional `read` query parameter:

- If `read` is omitted, the endpoint returns the complete book collection.
  This is the existing behavior and is the behavior used by the `All` view.
- If `read=true`, the endpoint returns only books whose `read` field is
  `true`.
- If `read=false`, the endpoint returns only books whose `read` field is
  `false`.

The client sends the values `true` and `false` in lowercase. The server must
interpret the parameter as a boolean filter rather than as a truthiness check
on an arbitrary non-empty string, so `false` must select unread books.

Every successful `GET /books` response retains the existing JSON shape:

```json
{
  "status": "success",
  "books": []
}
```

Only the contents of `books` vary with the filter. The response remains a
JSON collection, and the existing book object fields are unchanged. Filtering
must not mutate the stored collection or change its existing ordering.

The `POST /books` behavior and the `PUT` and `DELETE` behavior at
`/books/<book_id>` remain compatible with the existing API. Those operations
do not require a `read` query parameter; the Vue client applies its current
filter when it reloads after an operation.

## Vue client design

The component owns the active filter state and maps it to the API query:

- `all` produces an axios request without a `read` parameter.
- `read` produces `read=true`.
- `unread` produces `read=false`.

The collection-loading method is the single path used for initial loading,
filter changes, and post-CRUD refreshes. It reads the current filter state
when constructing each request. A response replaces the current `books`
collection, including replacing it with an empty array.

The initial lifecycle load uses `all`. A filter selection updates the active
state before loading so the selection remains correct even if the resulting
collection is empty. Add, update, and delete callbacks invoke the same
filtered loading path after the existing operation succeeds.

## Compatibility and boundaries

- A request to `GET /books` without `read` continues to return all books with
  the existing success envelope.
- Existing CRUD endpoints and payloads are not redesigned as part of this
  feature.
- The filter is a collection-view concern; it does not change the persisted
  `read` value of any book.
- Current user documentation is not updated by this specification task.

## Example interactions

### Initial page load

1. The page initializes its filter to `all`.
2. The client requests `GET /books`.
3. The server returns all books in the existing response shape.
4. The client renders the returned books with `All` active.

### Read view

1. The reader selects `Read`.
2. The client requests `GET /books?read=true`.
3. The server returns only books with `read: true`.
4. The client replaces the displayed collection and keeps `Read` active.

### Empty filtered view

1. The reader selects `Unread`.
2. The server returns `"books": []`.
3. The client clears any previous rows and displays the empty-result message
   while keeping `Unread` active.

### CRUD refresh in a filtered view

1. The reader selects `Read`.
2. The reader adds, updates, or deletes a book.
3. After the operation succeeds, the client requests
   `GET /books?read=true`.
4. The displayed collection reflects the server-filtered result and `Read`
   remains active.

needed to support it. It does not change the current user documentation or
the contracts of the existing create, update, and delete operations.

## Objective

Readers can switch the Books page between:

- All books
- Read books
- Unread books

The server remains the source of truth for the filtered collection. The Vue
client requests the selected collection rather than fetching all books and
filtering them locally.

## Vue client behavior

### Filter control and initial state

The Books page exposes one mutually exclusive filter control with the labels
`All`, `Read`, and `Unread`. The active option is visibly identifiable.

`All` is the initial selection. The initial collection request must therefore
be `GET /books` without a `read` query parameter.

Changing the selection updates the active option and requests the matching
collection:

| Selection | Request |
| --- | --- |
| All | `GET /books` |
| Read | `GET /books?read=true` |
| Unread | `GET /books?read=false` |

The client sends the lower-case query values shown above. It consumes the
response's existing `books` array; it does not apply a second client-side
filter.

### Refresh after a mutation

After a successful add, update, or delete, the Books page refreshes the list
using the currently selected filter. A mutation refresh must not reset the
selection to `All` or silently omit the `read` parameter when `Read` or
`Unread` is active.

This means a book changed by a mutation may stop appearing in the current
collection, and a newly added or updated book appears only when it matches
the active selection. The existing mutation endpoints, payloads, and success
flow remain unchanged.

### Empty results

When a successful filtered response contains an empty `books` array, the page
shows a clear, visible empty-state message such as `No books match the
selected filter.` The page must not communicate an empty result only through
an empty table. The previous collection must be replaced so stale rows are
not left visible.

The same empty-state treatment applies when the unfiltered `All` collection
is empty; the message may be phrased as `No books found.`.

`GET /books` accepts an optional `read` query parameter:

| Request | Collection returned |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /books` | Every book, preserving the current all-books behavior |
| `GET /books?read=true` | Books whose `read` field is `true` |
| `GET /books?read=false` | Books whose `read` field is `false` |

The parameter is optional. Omitting it is the compatibility path and must
return the same all-books collection semantics as the current endpoint.
`true` and `false` are the supported values generated by the client. No
client behavior depends on values outside that contract.

Filtering must happen on the Flask side before the response is serialized.
The order of books should remain the order of the underlying collection.

Every successful response keeps the existing JSON shape:

```json
{
  "status": "success",
  "books": [
    {
      "id": "1",
      "title": "On the Road",
      "author": "Jack Kerouac",
      "read": true
    }
  ]
}
```

The filter changes only the contents of `books`; it does not rename the
wrapper, remove `status`, or change the fields of a book. `POST /books`,
`PUT /books/<book_id>`, and `DELETE /books/<book_id>` retain their existing
routes and request/response contracts.

This feature does not add search, sorting, pagination, URL-based filter
persistence across a full page reload, or changes to the current user
documentation.

traceable acceptance criteria.
